In [[statistics]], the '''Chapman–Robbins bound''' or '''Hammersley–Chapman–Robbins bound''' is a lower bound on the [[variance]] of [[estimator]]s of a deterministic parameter. It is a generalization of the [[Cramér–Rao bound]]; compared to the Cramér–Rao bound, it is both tighter and applicable to a wider range of problems. However, it is usually more difficult to compute.

The bound was independently discovered by [[John Hammersley]] in 1950,<ref>{{Citation
  | last = Hammersley   | first = J. M. |authorlink=John Hammersley
  | title = On estimating restricted parameters
  | journal = Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B
  | volume = 12 | issue = 2 | pages = 192–240 | year = 1950
  | doi = 10.1111/j.2517-6161.1950.tb00056.x | mr = 40631
  | jstor = 2983981
}}</ref> and by Douglas Chapman and [[Herbert Robbins]] in 1951.<ref>{{Citation
  | last1 = Chapman | first1 =  D. G.
  | last2 = Robbins | first2 = H. | author2-link = Herbert Robbins
  | title = Minimum variance estimation without regularity assumptions
  | journal = [[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]]
  | volume = 22 | issue =4 | pages =581–586 | year =1951
  | doi = 10.1214/aoms/1177729548
  | mr = 44084
  | jstor = 2236927
| doi-access = free}}</ref>

== Statement ==
Let <math>\Theta</math> be the set of parameters for a family of probability distributions <math>\{\mu_\theta : \theta\in\Theta\}</math> on <math>\Omega</math>. 

For any two <math>\theta, \theta' \in \Theta</math>, let <math>\chi^2(\mu_{\theta'}; \mu_{\theta})</math> be the [[F-divergence#Instances_of_f-divergences|<math> \chi^2</math>-divergence]] from <math>\mu_{\theta}</math> to <math>\mu_{\theta'}</math>. Then:

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Given any scalar random variable <math>\hat g: \Omega \to \R</math>, and any <math>\theta \in\Theta</math>, we have
<math>\operatorname{Var}_\theta[\hat g] \geq \sup_{\theta'\neq \theta \in \Theta}\frac{(E_{\theta'}[\hat g] - E_{\theta}[\hat g])^2}{\chi^2(\mu_{\theta'} ; \mu_\theta)}</math>.
}}

A generalization to the multivariable case is:<ref name=":0" />

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Given any multivariate random variable <math>\hat g: \Omega \to \R^m</math>, and any <math>\theta, \theta' \in\Theta</math>, 
<math>\chi^2(\mu_{\theta'} ; \mu_\theta) \geq
(E_{\theta'}[\hat g] - E_{\theta}[\hat g])^T \operatorname{Cov}_\theta[\hat g]^{-1} (E_{\theta'}[\hat g] - E_{\theta}[\hat g])</math>
}}

== Proof ==
By the [[F-divergence#Basic variational representation|variational representation of chi-squared divergence]]:<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Polyanskiy |first=Yury |date=2017 |title=Lecture notes on information theory, chapter 29, ECE563 (UIUC) |url=https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/LN_stats.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220524014051/https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/LN_stats.pdf |archive-date=2022-05-24 |access-date=2022-05-24 |website=Lecture notes on information theory}}</ref><math display="block">\chi^2(P; Q) = \sup_g \frac{(E_P[g]-E_Q[g])^2}{\operatorname{Var}_Q[g]}</math>
Plug in <math>g = \hat g, P = \mu_{\theta'}, Q = \mu_\theta</math>, to obtain: <math display="block">\chi^2(\mu_{\theta'}; \mu_\theta) \geq \frac{(E_{\theta'}[\hat g]-E_\theta[\hat g])^2}{\operatorname{Var}_\theta[\hat g]}</math>Switch the denominator and the left side and take supremum over <math>\theta'</math> to obtain the single-variate case. For the multivariate case, we define <math display="inline">h = \sum_{i=1}^m v_i \hat g_i</math> for any <math>v\neq 0 \in \R^m</math>. Then plug in <math>g = h</math> in the variational representation to obtain: <math display="block">\chi^2(\mu_{\theta'}; \mu_\theta) \geq \frac{(E_{\theta'}[h]-E_\theta[h])^2}{\operatorname{Var}_\theta[h]} = \frac{\langle v, E_{\theta'}[\hat g]-E_\theta[\hat g]\rangle^2}{v^T \operatorname{Cov}_\theta[\hat g] v} </math>Take supremum over <math>v\neq 0 \in\R^m </math>, using the [[linear algebra]] fact that <math>\sup_{v\neq 0} \frac{v^T ww^T v}{v^T M v} = w^T M^{-1}w </math>, we obtain the multivariate case.

== Relation to Cramér–Rao bound ==
Usually, <math>\Omega = \mathcal X^n</math> is the [[sample space]] of <math>n</math> independent draws of a <math>\mathcal X</math>-valued [[random variable]] <math>X</math> with distribution <math>\lambda_\theta</math> from a by <math>\theta \in \Theta \subseteq \mathbb R^m</math> parameterized family of probability distributions, <math>\mu_\theta = \lambda_\theta^{\otimes n}</math> is its <math>n</math>-fold [[product measure]], and <math>\hat g : \mathcal X^n \to \Theta</math> is an estimator of <math>\theta</math>. Then, for <math>m=1</math>, the expression inside the supremum in the Chapman–Robbins bound converges to the [[Cramér–Rao bound]] of <math>\hat g</math> when <math>\theta' \to \theta</math>, assuming the regularity conditions of the Cramér–Rao bound hold. This implies that, when both bounds exist, the Chapman–Robbins version is always at least as tight as the Cramér–Rao bound; in many cases, it is substantially tighter. 

The Chapman–Robbins bound also holds under much weaker regularity conditions. For example, no assumption is made regarding differentiability of the [[probability density function]] ''p''(''x''; ''θ'') of <math>\lambda_\theta</math>. When ''p''(''x''; ''θ'') is non-differentiable, the [[Fisher information]] is not defined, and hence the Cramér–Rao bound does not exist.
